prize_parts.citation: For the theoretical prediction of time-reversal-invariant topological insulators and the quantum spin Hall effect, and for their first experimental realisation in HgTe quantum wells

statement.case_for: B038 is a concept-level discovery: a new topological classification (Z2) of time-reversal-invariant band insulators, with protected helical edge and surface states that follow from symmetry rather than from detail. Kane and Mele supplied the idea and the invariant, and Molenkamp's HgTe experiment showed that nature realises it, including the conductance signature of the edge channels. The idea has since been confirmed independently in several material families (HgTe, InAs/GaSb, Bi-Sb and Bi2Se3 by ARPES) and has changed how band structures are classified and searched for. It is broad, mathematically clean and about two decades old, so maturity is not in question. As someone who works with universality and emergent structure, I find that an organising principle that survives across materials is exactly what the prize should reward. Four others ranked it in their top four, which is more cross-member support than most items on this list, but I weigh the science rather than the tally.
statement.case_against: The credit chain is incomplete. Bernevig, Hughes and Zhang made the specific HgTe proposal that Molenkamp's group tested, and the 3D topological insulator theory and ARPES work (Fu, Kane, Mele; Moore and Balents; Hsieh, Hasan) lie outside the three credited names, so a prize here will be argued to be either too narrow or unfair to those left out. The 2016 prize on topological phase transitions and topological phases of matter will also make some colleagues see this as a continuation. Finally, graphene's spin-orbit gap is too small for the original Kane-Mele model to be observed there, so the clean story is 'prediction in graphene, realisation in HgTe', which needs careful citation wording.

responses.point: Olle ranks B042 (magic-angle graphene) first, values the simple band-structure idea that predicts an interaction-dominated regime, and also puts B038 third while flagging the omission of Bernevig, Hughes and Zhang and closeness to the 2016 topological prize.
responses.response: I agree with the attribution worry; it is the real weakness of B038, and I would not claim it is solved by the credited trio. Where I differ is on closeness to 2016: Thouless, Haldane and Kosterlitz were rewarded for topological phase transitions and the Hall-type topological phases, whereas Z2 invariants protected by time-reversal symmetry, with no external field, are a distinct classification, and the HgTe experiment settled it. On B042 I accept the originality and the number of groups working on it, but the pairing mechanism for the superconductivity is unsettled and the field is younger, so I rank it below B038 on maturity. I would keep it as an alternative rather than drop it.

responses.point: Eva Lindroth ranks B038 third but says the credit is partial: Bernevig, Hughes and Zhang are missing, the 3D route is outside this entry, and graphene's spin-orbit gap may be too small to count as a verified realisation.
responses.response: The graphene point is correct and I accept it, which is why my citation names HgTe quantum wells as the realisation and does not claim Kane-Mele graphene was observed. I partly disagree that the missing proposers make the credit unfair: the Z2 invariant and the quantum spin Hall state in Kane and Mele are the conceptual origin, and the HgTe proposal applies it to a particular material, so the theory credit to Kane and Mele is defensible. I concede that the committee could reasonably look hard at the HgTe proposal, and I would welcome a discussion of this before the final ballot.

responses.point: Stefan Kroll ranks the optical lattice clock (B046) first as the clearest case where a technique changed what can be measured, with high maturity and a clean two-name credit, and notes overlap with earlier prizes on combs and ion clocks.
responses.response: I take the clean two-name credit and the reproducibility seriously, and B046 is my first alternative. My reservation is on novelty: Katori and Ye's clocks are a spectacular refinement of a technology line already recognised in 2005 and 2012, and the redefinition of the second has not yet happened. B038 introduces a new organising idea in condensed matter, with a less tidy attribution. Both are mature; I would weigh a new concept above a record-setting instrument when the committee has recently recognised the instrument's lineage, but I accept that this is a judgement about prize philosophy and not an objective ranking.

responses.point: Eva Olsson ranks B042 (twisted bilayer graphene) first because of its falsifiable theory prediction and downstream impact, and ranks B038 sixth.
responses.response: I do not dispute the downstream impact of B042, and the Bistritzer-MacDonald prediction followed by the 2018 experiments is a model of theory and experiment fitting together. But the interpretation of the correlated phases, particularly superconductivity, is still contested, and the prize would have to be written around the flat-band prediction and observed correlated insulators. B038 has more than a decade of additional independent confirmation across materials. I would want to hear why you rank B038 as low as sixth, whether on credit or on novelty after 2016.

uncertainties: Whether Bernevig, Hughes and Zhang must be credited for the HgTe quantum-spin-Hall proposal, and whether the committee can do this within a three-person limit.
Whether the prize should cover only the 2D quantum spin Hall effect or also the 3D topological insulators, which would involve names outside the credited set.
How much weight to give the 2016 prize when judging whether this is a distinct achievement.
I am recalling priority details from memory and have not verified them.
statement.conflict_note: No specific conflict is apparent from my provided profile: none of the credited names for B038, B046 or B042 appears among my documented co-authors, supervisors or institutions. My work on stochastic processes and neural networks is not close to any shortlisted topic.
